fatality_rate.notes: Symptomatic case-fatality rate for seasonal influenza is low and varies substantially by season severity and age group. Mortality is heavily concentrated in adults 65+ (about two-thirds of deaths in recent U.S. seasons) and is far lower in children and young adults. The typical value (0.07%) reflects symptomatic-case denominators for seasonal influenza. Case definition drives fatality rate estimates by orders of magnitude: a systematic review of the 2009 H1N1 pandemic found estimates ranging from ~0.001-0.01% using an infections denominator, ~0-1.2% using a symptomatic-cases denominator, and ~0-13.5% using a laboratory-confirmed-cases denominator, with the latter most prone to ascertainment bias since testing is typically reserved for more severe presentations. Any fatality rate figure should be interpreted alongside its denominator definition.

fatality_rate.notes: Fatality is high without treatment (historically ~50-80%) but drops sharply with prompt antibiotic therapy to roughly 10-15% overall. U.S. age-stratified data (1998-2007) shows a clear age gradient even among treated cases: 6% in infants <1 year, 9.7% in adolescents 14-17, and 13.6% in young adults 18-24 — the opposite pattern from raw incidence, which is highest in infants. Recent surveillance also found an unusually high 18% fatality rate for an emerging serogroup Y strain (2023-2024), compared to 11% in the preceding 2017-2021 period.

immunity_duration.notes: Natural immunity is continuously reinforced by intermittent carriage rather than following a single post-infection decay curve (see estimates below). Vaccine-induced immunity duration differs by vaccine type: CDC's booster schedule implies MenACWY protection lasts roughly 4-5 years before meaningful waning (booster at 16 after initial dose at 11-12; every-5-year boosters for ongoing high risk), while MenB protection appears shorter-lived, with boosters recommended as early as 1-3 years post-series, or within 6-12 months during active outbreaks. Antibody-persistence cohort studies (Zangwill et al.) found vaccine-induced bactericidal activity detectable up to 10 years post-vaccination, though substantially declined by year 2.

r0.notes: Estimates vary enormously by transmission setting rather than clustering around one 'general population' value, since most HAV transmission is fecal-oral/foodborne rather than driven by the direct-contact networks these R0 estimates characterize. Close-contact/direct-transmission outbreaks among naive children (e.g., schools) show R0 of 1.9-2.5; modeling of sexual/close-contact transmission in high-risk adult populations (MSM) spans 1.71-3.67. People who inject drugs (PWID) — a leading driver of recent U.S. person-to-person HAV outbreaks — show the widest and often highest state-level estimates (2.2-5.0 across 16 US states), with a pooled herd immunity threshold of 64% (90% prediction interval: 52-76%), reflecting dense, frequent direct-contact/sharing networks.

estimate_extremes.title: Ebola RNA Persistence in Semen of Ebola Virus Disease Survivors — Final Report

infectious_days.notes: Patients are not infectious during incubation — infectiousness begins with symptom onset and rises with viral load as illness progresses, so the effective infectious window runs from onset until isolation, recovery, or death. Untreated, mean time from onset to death is roughly 7-8 days and onset to recovery roughly 11-12 days, but isolation typically truncates community exposure well before either endpoint. Two features break the simple SEIR framing: corpses are highly infectious and traditional burial washing has driven a large share of transmission, effectively extending the infectious period past death; and viral RNA persists in immune-privileged sites in survivors, with semen positive for many months (documented sexual transmission more than a year after recovery) and rare relapse with CNS or ocular involvement. Models that ignore the post-death and post-recovery channels will understate tail transmission.

Ebola disease distribution by species and outbreak

fatality_rate.notes: Among the highest CFRs of any human pathogen, but the range is enormous and driven more by care setting and species than by anything intrinsic to a given outbreak. Species ordering is consistent: Zaire ebolavirus is the most lethal (roughly 60-90% historically), Sudan ebolavirus intermediate (roughly 40-60%), Bundibugyo ebolavirus lowest (roughly 25-40%). Reston ebolavirus has caused no known human illness. Supportive care matters enormously — aggressive fluid and electrolyte management alone cut mortality substantially in the 2014-2016 epidemic, and the monoclonal antibody therapeutics (mAb114 / ansuvimab and REGN-EB3 / inmazeb) proven in the 2018-2020 DRC PALM trial reduced mortality to roughly 30% overall and into the single digits among patients treated early with low viral load. Reported outbreak CFRs are also inflated or deflated by outcome ascertainment: cases lost to follow-up are disproportionately survivors in some datasets and disproportionately deaths in others.

average_contacts_daily.notes: Not meaningfully captured by a general daily-contacts metric. Transmission requires direct contact with blood, vomit, stool, or other body fluids from a symptomatic patient or a corpse, so conversational-contact surveys such as POLYMOD are a poor proxy — the relevant exposure set is caregivers, burial participants, and unprotected health workers, not the general contact network. The usual substitutes in the literature are household secondary attack rate (pooled at roughly 12-17%, rising sharply with the intimacy of care provided) and funeral attendance, and transmission is strongly overdispersed at the individual level. If a contact-network model is required, parameterize on household and care-contact structure plus discrete funeral events rather than on a mean daily contact count.

estimate_extremes.title: Ebola disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus

immunity_duration.notes: Survivors of natural infection carry detectable IgG for decades, and no well-documented case of reinfection with the same species has been reported, so natural immunity is generally treated as long-lasting to lifelong. Antibody persistence is not the same as demonstrated protection — the decades-long evidence is serological, since challenge studies are impossible and reinfection exposure is rare. Cross-protection between species (Zaire, Sudan, Bundibugyo) is limited and should not be assumed; the licensed rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine (Ervebo) targets Zaire ebolavirus only and offers no reliable protection against Sudan ebolavirus, which is why the 2022 Uganda Sudan-virus outbreak had no licensed vaccine available.
immunity_duration.special_value: lifelong; natural infection: likely lifelong or multi-decade; vaccine: at least 2-4 years, durability beyond that not established

asymptomatic_fraction.notes: The single most contested parameter for this pathogen, with credible published estimates spanning more than an order of magnitude. The disagreement is largely methodological: seroprevalence studies in contacts pick up antibody-positive people who never reported illness, but Ebola serological assays have known specificity problems in populations with high background reactivity, and recall of mild illness months after an epidemic is poor. Studies using stricter case definitions and better-validated assays tend to land far lower than the early Gabon work. Consequential modeling caveat: asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic individuals are not believed to transmit, since infectiousness tracks viral load and symptom severity — so unlike most respiratory pathogens, a high asymptomatic fraction here reduces the susceptible pool without adding hidden transmission chains. Setting this parameter high therefore makes outbreaks easier to control in most model structures, which is the opposite of the usual intuition and worth checking explicitly in sensitivity analysis.

r0.note: Typical value taken from mean of systematic review of multiple countries with over 2000 studies reviewed.

infectious_days.note: Patients are not infectious during incubation — infectiousness begins with symptom onset and rises with viral load as illness progresses, so the effective infectious window runs from onset until isolation, recovery, or death. Untreated, mean time from onset to death is roughly 7-8 days and onset to recovery roughly 11-12 days, but isolation typically truncates community exposure well before either endpoint. Two features break the simple SEIR framing: corpses are highly infectious and traditional burial washing has driven a large share of transmission, effectively extending the infectious period past death; and viral RNA persists in immune-privileged sites in survivors, with semen positive for many months (documented sexual transmission more than a year after recovery) and rare relapse with CNS or ocular involvement. Models that ignore the post-death and post-recovery channels will understate tail transmission.
